attempts.label: DANDI:000253
attempts.paper_title: Survey of spiking in the mouse visual system reveals functional hierarchy
attempts.entry_title: Survey of spiking in the mouse visual system (Siegle, Jia et al. 2021), from its DANDI deposits
attempts.description: Tests the findings of Siegle, Jia et al. (2021) for dandiset 000253, which names the paper but holds a different experiment (the OpenScope Global/Local Oddball project). The passive viewing claims are tested on the paper's own deposits, dandisets 000021 and 000022 (58 sessions), with receptive fields, latencies, modulation indices, timescales and jitter-corrected cross-correlograms recomputed from the spike times, and the behaviour claims on the metrics tables of the paper's GitHub repository.

notebooks.title: Unit counts, receptive fields, Figure 3 metrics, behaviour tables and gaze
Cross-correlogram claims (Figure 2, Extended Data Figures 7, 8 and 10)

outcomes.statement: Of 87 mice entering the recording step, 61 passed session-level quality control and 58 resulted in NWB files; these 58 passive viewing experiments are the ones analysed.
outcomes.source: Results, A survey of visually evoked spiking, paragraph 2; Methods, Quality control for the Neuropixels recording session; Methods, Data processing pipeline
outcomes.quote: reducing the number of experiments analysed and presented here from 87 to 58
outcomes.notes: 000021 and 000022 hold 58 sessions of 58 mice, 30 wild type and 8 Pvalb, 12 Sst and 8 Vip Cre lines crossed with Ai32. The pipeline counts before release (87, 61) are not judged.
deviations: Tested on dandisets 000021 and 000022, where the paper deposited these data; dandiset 000253 holds a different experiment.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: 284 of the 332 probes were mapped to the CCFv3.
outcomes.source: Methods, Neuropixels recordings, Probes; Methods, Ex vivo imaging quality control
outcomes.quote: In total, 284 out of 332 probes were mapped to the CCFv3
outcomes.notes: The 58 sessions hold 332 probes; 284 have a positive sum of anterior-posterior CCF coordinates over the units passing the three quality filters, as ExtDataFigure1jk.py counts, and the other 48 have no CCF coordinate on any unit. Reading (a), the 58 released sessions.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: After quality filtering, 682 +/- 144 units were recorded per experiment, 119 +/- 48 per probe and 56 +/- 30 per visual area, with 6.1 +/- 1.1 visual areas sampled per experiment.
outcomes.source: Results, A survey of visually evoked spiking, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 1j, k
outcomes.quote: Overall, we recorded 682 ± 144 units per experiment, 119 ± 48 units per probe and 56 ± 30 units per visual area ( Extended Data Fig. 1j ), sampling 6.1 ± 1.1 visual areas per experiment
outcomes.notes: Units per experiment 686.2 +/- 144.6, per probe 128.8 +/- 51.1, per area per experiment 56.2 +/- 30.3 (352 experiment-area pairs), areas per experiment 6.07 +/- 1.13. All within tolerance.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Units in the eight visual areas were highly visually responsive, 60% having a significant spatial receptive field within the monitor, against only 1.4% of units in the hippocampus (CA1, CA3 and dentate gyrus).
outcomes.source: Results, A survey of visually evoked spiking, paragraph 3; Fig. 1g
outcomes.quote: Units recorded in all eight cortical and thalamic visual areas were highly visually responsive, with 60% displaying significant spatial receptive fields within the boundaries of the monitor ... and found them in only 1.4% of units
outcomes.notes: 26,694 of 43,990 non-noise units of the eight areas (60.7%) have p < 0.01. In CA1, CA3 and DG 415 of 26,289 (1.58%) do pooled, and 1.71% on the mean over 52 mice; both readings are outside 1.4% +/- 0.14%. The criterion names no partial outcome; the 60% holds and the hippocampal fraction is near the paper's but outside its tolerance, so the claim holds in part. Without the 10-spike rule 60.8%, 1.61% and 1.74%; with the units without a p-value left out of the denominator 67.2%, 1.81% and 1.94%. The fraction in the eight areas is 55.4% at p < 0.001 and 62.5% at p < 0.02; in the hippocampus 1.03% at p < 0.005 and 2.58% at p < 0.02.
deviations: The p-value is computed from the spike times as the Methods describe (the AllenSDK value the figure code reads is not in the NWB files). Shuffles stop once 10 of them reach the observed statistic, which settles p >= 0.01; the threshold decision is the same as with 1,000.

As the AllenSDK's ReceptiveFieldMapping (github.com/AllenInstitute/AllenSDK, tag v2.0.0, commit 5200c742, minimum_spike_count=10.0), the code the paper names for its stimulus metrics, a unit with fewer than 10 spikes over all Gabor presentations has no p-value and counts as not significant, as Figure1g.py counts it. The AllenSDK resamples presentations with replacement for its null; the Methods' location shuffles are used.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: The paper's per-unit tables (data/time_to_first_spike.csv, data/timescale_metrics.csv and data/layer_info.csv) describe the units of dandisets 000021 and 000022, matched by ecephys unit id.
outcomes.source: Code availability; common/create_units_table.py of the paper's repository
outcomes.notes: All ids of the three tables (99,180, 23,524 and 99,180 rows) are non-noise units of the dandisets; 664 non-noise units are absent from the layer table. Recomputed timescales agree with timescale_metrics.csv (99.3% of 23,352 units within 1% for the response decay timescale, 99.6% of 21,122 for the intrinsic timescale). Recomputed latencies do not agree with time_to_first_spike.csv; with a 200 ms window 16.1% of 62,483 units are within 1 ms, median absolute difference 4.0 ms, median signed difference -0.5 ms, and the 250 ms, dark, light and 500 ms readings 3.0% to 13.6%. On one session (1,591 units) none of 60 procedures (window ends 100 to 500 ms, all flashes or one half, median or mean) brings more than 14.5% within 1 ms. No script of the repository writes the latency table; Figure3/get_flash_PSTH.py reads it and writes a different file. Layer codes 1, 2 and 3 are also given to CA1, CA2 and CA3 units; with cortical_depth > 0 only VIS* units remain. ed10b and ed10ce use the layer table only, whose ids link fully.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability), with GitHub AllenInstitute/neuropixels_platform_paper at commit 4f8bcc26fa6fbec1ae687c650bacc9ea67a7036d

outcomes.statement: The mean time to first spike after a full-field flash in each area is correlated with its anatomical hierarchy score.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 4; Fig. 3a to c
outcomes.quote: the mean visual latency of each area was correlated with its anatomical hierarchy score ( Fig. 3c ; Pearson’s r = 0.95, P = 0.00025)
outcomes.notes: All flashes, 250 ms window, 13,344 units; area means 66.1 ms (V1) to 75.2 ms (PM), r = 0.959, p = 0.0002. Dark flashes r = 0.904 (p = 0.002), light r = 0.933 (p = 0.0007), so the three readings agree. Variants; 500 ms window r = 0.802, 200 ms r = 0.936, the paper's table r = 0.953.
deviations: Unit metrics (p_value_rf, area_rf, firing_rate_dg) recomputed from spike times; the paper read them from the AllenSDK.
The claims file names the flashes as open; Figure3/get_flash_PSTH.py uses every flash presentation (fl.stim_table.index.values), so all flashes is the main reading.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Latencies differ significantly between all pairs of areas except LGN-V1, RL-LP, LP-AL and AM-PM.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 9a
outcomes.quote: Statistical testing revealed significantly different latencies for all pairs of areas, except for LGN–V1, RL–LP, LP–AL and AM–PM
outcomes.notes: LGN-V1, RL-LP, LP-AL and PM-AM are not significant (corrected p 0.44 to 0.90), and RL-AL is not significant either (0.52); 27 of 28 pairs agree. Dark flashes also give one disagreement (LGN-LM); light flashes four.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Receptive field size increases with anatomical hierarchy score.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 4; Fig. 3d to f
outcomes.quote: found a systematic increase in receptive field size with anatomical hierarchy score ( Fig. 3d - f ; Pearson’s r = 0.97, P = 8.3 × 10 −5 )
outcomes.notes: Mean RF area 544 deg2 (LGN) to 905 deg2 (AM), 13,344 units; r = 0.958, p = 0.0002. Without the latency cut r = 0.974. Brain Observatory sessions alone r = 0.957, Functional Connectivity r = 0.913.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Receptive field sizes differ significantly between all pairs of areas except LM-RL.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 9d
outcomes.quote: Statistical testing revealed significantly different receptive field sizes for all pairs of areas, except for LM–RL
outcomes.notes: LM-RL is not significant (corrected p = 0.41) as stated; LM-AL (0.38) and RL-AL (0.067) are not significant either. 26 of 28 pairs agree.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: The modulation index of responses to drifting gratings is highest in LGN and decreases along the hierarchy.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 4; Fig. 3g to i
outcomes.quote: The modulation index was highest in the LGN, whereas higher areas showed gradually less phase-dependent modulation ( Fig. 3g - i , Pearson’s r = −0.89, P = 0.003)
outcomes.notes: Mean log10 MI highest in LGN (0.628), lowest in AM (-0.124); r = -0.954, p = 0.0002. The mean of MI gives r = -0.934; each stimulus set alone gives r = -0.911 and -0.963, LGN highest.
deviations: Assumed - the preferred condition is the drifting grating condition (orientation, temporal frequency, and contrast in the Functional Connectivity set) with the highest mean spike count, blanks excluded. The paper takes MI from the AllenSDK and does not define the preferred condition; this is the AllenSDK's usual definition.
Welch spectrum with nperseg 256 on the 2 s PSTH of 200 bins, as functions/modulation_index.py.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Modulation indices differ significantly between all pairs of areas except RL-AL and AM-PM.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 9e
outcomes.quote: Statistical tests revealed significantly different modulation indices for all pairs of areas, except for RL–AL and AM–PM
outcomes.notes: PM-AM is not significant (corrected p = 0.12) as stated, but RL-AL is significant (0.0006), and LM-RL (0.63), LM-LP (0.88) and RL-LP (0.54) are not. 4 of 28 pairs disagree.
deviations: The same assumed preferred condition as fig3i-modulation-index-hierarchy.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: The mean intrinsic timescale of spontaneous activity in each area is not correlated with the visual hierarchy.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 9f, g
outcomes.quote: this mean intrinsic timescale for each area was not correlated with the visual hierarchy ( Extended Data Fig. 9f , g ) (Pearson’s r = −0.24, P = 0.57)
outcomes.notes: 15,958 units kept (SD < 100, at least 100 spikes); area means 23.6 to 40.1 ms; r = -0.158, p = 0.71. The code's window (1.0 to 2.0 s after onset, 5 to 400 ms) gives r = -0.290, p = 0.49. The test is weak; 8,834 of the 15,958 kept units sit at the 1 ms lower bound of the fit (median 1.00 ms), and without them r = 0.082, p = 0.85.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Higher-order areas have a longer response decay timescale during the flash response, and the area mean correlates with hierarchy score.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 4; Fig. 3j to l
outcomes.quote: Higher-order areas had a longer response decay timescale, and therefore maintain stimulus-evoked activity over longer temporal windows, than lower stages ... ( Fig. 3j - l ; Pearson’s r = 0.86, P = 0.007)
outcomes.notes: Methods window 0 to 250 ms, 5,842 units - r = 0.804, p = 0.016, PM 53.3 and AM 54.6 ms highest. The code's 40 to 290 ms window gives r = 0.876 (7,467 units), the paper's tables r = 0.855.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Response decay timescales differ significantly between all pairs of areas except LM-AL and AM-PM.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 4; Extended Data Fig. 9h
outcomes.quote: Statistical testing revealed significantly distinct response decay timescales for all pairs of areas, except for LM–AL and AM–PM
outcomes.notes: With the Methods' window PM-AM is not significant (corrected p = 0.28) as stated, but LM-AL is (0.018), and LGN-LM (0.068), LGN-AL (0.81) and RL-LP (0.064) are not; 4 of 28 disagree. With the code's 40 to 290 ms window only LGN-V1 disagrees, which would be partially reproduced. Which window the paper used is asked of its authors (see findings).
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: The Figure 3 analyses use 15,713 units from 58 mice, and the response decay timescale 7,837 units.
outcomes.source: Fig. 3 legend
outcomes.quote: n = 7,837 units from 58 mice ... n = 15,713 units from 58 mice unless otherwise specified
outcomes.notes: With the claims' procedure (latency within the Methods' 250 ms, decay timescale over 0 to 250 ms) 13,344 units after the latency cut (reading a) and 24,459 before it (reading b), against 15,713 +/- 1,571, and 5,842 for the decay timescale against 7,837 +/- 784. Variants, not judged; the scripts' windows (200 ms; 40 to 290 ms) give 17,163 and 8,381, the paper's tables 15,849 and 7,798, all within tolerance. The round-1 record adopted the scripts' windows on the reading that get_flash_PSTH.py wrote the paper's latency table; it reads that table, so the claims file's reading is kept. Which windows the paper used is asked of its authors (see findings). Without the firing_rate_dg > 0.1 Hz cut, whose definition is assumed, 13,476 and 25,019; the cut removes 560 units and does not change the outcome.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Time to first spike measured in the grey pre-stimulus interval is not correlated with hierarchy score but is strongly negatively correlated with baseline firing rate, so firing rate does not explain the latency result.
outcomes.source: Methods, Response latency; Extended Data Fig. 9b, c
outcomes.quote: Under these conditions, TFS for individual areas was not correlated with anatomical hierarchy score (Pearson’s r = 0.57, P = 0.14), but was strongly negatively correlated with their baseline firing rates (Pearson’s r = −0.98, P = 0.00001

statistics.about: spontaneous time to first spike against hierarchy score
spontaneous time to first spike against baseline firing rate

outcomes.notes: Spontaneous latency against hierarchy r = 0.290, p = 0.49 (no correlation, as stated); against the pre-flash rate (reading a) r = -0.991, p = 2e-06; against the overall rate (b) r = -0.987. 156 of 13,344 units have no spontaneous latency.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Overall firing rate does not correlate with hierarchy score, so the four metrics do not depend on it.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 9i, j
outcomes.quote: These metrics are not dependent on overall firing rate, which does not correlate with hierarchy score ( Extended Data Fig. 9i , j )
outcomes.notes: Mean log10 rate r = -0.327, p = 0.43; mean rate r = -0.363, p = 0.38.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Compared with deep layers (5 and 6), superficial layers (2/3 and 4) have an earlier time to first spike, smaller receptive fields, a higher modulation index and a faster response decay timescale.
outcomes.source: Extended Data Fig. 10b legend; Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 5
outcomes.quote: On average, in comparison to deep layers (5 and 6), superficial layers (2/3 and 4) had an earlier time to first spike (2.59 ms difference, P = 2.7 × 10 −19 , two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test), smaller receptive fields (109° difference, P = 1.1 × 10 −33 ), higher modulation index (0.09 MI difference, P = 5.0 × 10 −23 ), and faster response decay timescale (6.6 ms difference, P = 3.8 × 10 −33 )

statistics.about: time to first spike, superficial against deep
receptive field area, superficial against deep
response decay timescale, superficial against deep

outcomes.notes: With the claims' procedure (the Methods' windows), deep minus superficial 1.34 ms latency (expected 2.59 +/- 0.26), 105 deg2 RF area (109 +/- 10.9) and 7.71 ms decay timescale (6.6 +/- 0.66), superficial minus deep 0.117 log10 MI (0.09 +/- 0.009); all four have the stated sign with p < 1e-4, and only the RF area is within tolerance, 1 of 4 parts. Raw MI gives 0.587. The code's layer split and the six areas alone change the differences by at most 0.09 ms, 4.3 deg2, 0.010 and 0.13 ms. Variants, not judged; the scripts' windows give 2.80 ms, 113 deg2, 0.127 and 6.39 ms, the paper's tables 2.55 ms, 110 deg2, 0.124 and 6.69 ms, 3 of 4 parts each.
deviations: The pool of all cortical units with a depth includes VIS, VISmma, VISli and VISmmp units, as the code's commented-out area line implies.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: In the anatomical hierarchy recomputed from ref. 3, LGN is lowest, then V1, with LM, RL, LP and AL at intermediate levels and PM and AM at the top; all areas have significantly different scores except RL and LM.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 1; Fig. 2a, b; Methods, Anatomical hierarchy analysis
outcomes.quote: The LGN sits at the bottom of the hierarchy, followed by its major target structure, V1; areas LM, RL, LP and AL reside at intermediate levels, and areas PM and AM occupy the top level of the areas we studied here

statistics.about: RL against LM, bootstrapped hierarchy scores
statistics.n: 100 bootstrap samples of the connectivity data

outcomes.notes: The scores in Figure3/Figure3.py order the areas LGN, V1, LM, RL, LP, AL, PM, AM. The bootstrap test of RL against LM needs the connectivity data of ref. 3 and was not run, so the part of the statement about significant differences is not tested.
outcomes.where: Connectivity data of Harris et al. 2019, Nature 575, 195-202, doi:10.1038/s41586-019-1716-z (ref. 3)

outcomes.statement: Mice performed the change detection task with high hit and low false alarm rates (mean hit rate 0.78, false alarm rate 0.13, d-prime 2.0 +/- 0.1 in 12 mice, 21 sessions).
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 6; Fig. 4b
outcomes.quote: Mice performed with high hit and low false alarm rates (mean hit rate = 0.78, mean false alarm rate = 0.13, and mean detection sensitivity ( d′ ) = 2.0 ± 0.1, in 12 mice, 21 sessions
outcomes.notes: The 21 behaviour sessions are not in dandiset 000253 (an oddball experiment without a task) nor in 000021 or 000022 (passive viewing only), and the paper names no deposit for them; its repository holds only per-unit and per-session metrics, without licks or trials.

outcomes.statement: During behaviour the first spike latency of image responses is correlated with the anatomical hierarchy score.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 6; Fig. 4e
outcomes.quote: the first spike latency for image responses during behaviour was correlated with the anatomical hierarchy score ( Fig. 4e )
outcomes.notes: From change_modulation_data.csv, means from 60.1 ms (LGd) to 77.2 ms (PM); r = 0.917, p = 0.0013.
outcomes.where: GitHub AllenInstitute/neuropixels_platform_paper, commit 4f8bcc26fa6fbec1ae687c650bacc9ea67a7036d, data/change_modulation_data.csv

outcomes.statement: During active behaviour the change modulation index is positive in every area and increases along the hierarchy from LGN to AM, and it is larger during active behaviour than during passive replay.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 7; Fig. 4f
outcomes.quote: During active behaviour, CMI was positive for each area ... More importantly, CMI systematically increased along the hierarchy from the LGN to the AM ( Fig. 4f ; Pearson’s r = 0.83, P = 0.011) ... CMI values were larger during active behaviour compared with passive viewing of the same stimulus sequence
outcomes.notes: Active CMI r = 0.828, p = 0.011; positive in all eight areas (0.111 to 0.312); above the passive mean in all eight areas (means 0.221 and 0.140), so both readings of part 3 hold.
outcomes.where: GitHub AllenInstitute/neuropixels_platform_paper, commit 4f8bcc26fa6fbec1ae687c650bacc9ea67a7036d, data/change_modulation_data.csv

outcomes.statement: The change modulation index correlates with hierarchy on hit trials but not on miss trials.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 7; Extended Data Fig. 9k
outcomes.quote: we found a significant correlation of CMI with hierarchy on hit but not on miss trials ( Extended Data Fig. 9k ; hit trials, Pearson’s r = 0.85, P = 0.007; miss trials, Pearson’s r = 0.51, P = 0.2)
outcomes.where: GitHub AllenInstitute/neuropixels_platform_paper, commit 4f8bcc26fa6fbec1ae687c650bacc9ea67a7036d, data/change_modulation_data.csv

outcomes.statement: Baseline firing rate, the response to the pre-change image and the response to the change image during the task are not correlated with hierarchy score.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 7; Extended Data Fig. 9l to n
outcomes.quote: Other aspects of neural activity during the task ... including the baseline firing rate, response to the pre-change image and the response to the change image ... were not correlated with hierarchy score
outcomes.notes: Active baseline r = -0.584 (p = 0.13), pre-change r = -0.239 (0.57), change r = 0.107 (0.80). The passive columns are not significant either (p 0.079 to 0.66).
outcomes.where: GitHub AllenInstitute/neuropixels_platform_paper, commit 4f8bcc26fa6fbec1ae687c650bacc9ea67a7036d, data/change_modulation_data.csv

outcomes.statement: The trial-wise covariation of change decoder output with the mouse's choices increases along the hierarchy, starting with no correlation in LGN.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 8; Fig. 4g, h
outcomes.quote: we found a strong increase in trial-wise decoder-behaviour covariation at higher levels of the hierarchy, starting with no correlation at the level of the LGN ( Fig. 4h ; Pearson’s r = 0.88, P = 0.004
outcomes.notes: r = 0.881, p = 0.0038; LGN -0.015 +/- 0.032 (3 sessions) includes zero.
outcomes.where: GitHub AllenInstitute/neuropixels_platform_paper, commit 4f8bcc26fa6fbec1ae687c650bacc9ea67a7036d, data/decoding_data.csv

outcomes.statement: Change decoders trained on 20 units performed better than chance in all eight areas, and decoder accuracy was not correlated with hierarchy score.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 8; Extended Data Fig. 9p and its legend
outcomes.quote: Decoders were separately trained for 20 units within each area and performed significantly better than chance across trials, indicating that change trials could be read out from all 8 areas ... Decoder accuracy for each brain region (mean ± s.e.m., averaged across sessions) is not correlated with the anatomical hierarchy score
outcomes.notes: Mean accuracy 0.688 to 0.835; mean minus s.e.m. above 0.5 and one-sided p < 0.05 in all eight areas (largest p 0.003, LP); accuracy against hierarchy r = 0.566, p = 0.14.
outcomes.where: GitHub AllenInstitute/neuropixels_platform_paper, commit 4f8bcc26fa6fbec1ae687c650bacc9ea67a7036d, data/decoding_data.csv

outcomes.statement: Across 50 mice with eye tracking, 95% of gaze locations fell within 6.4 +/- 2.1 degrees of the mean, with a maximum of 13.6 degrees.
outcomes.source: Methods, Eye and pupil tracking
outcomes.quote: On average, 95% of gaze locations fell within 6.4 ± 2.1° of the mean, with a maximum of 13.6°
outcomes.notes: 50 sessions have gaze mapping. Radial 95% distance from the mean gaze 6.59 +/- 2.18 degrees, maximum 14.29 (reading a); per axis 6.21 +/- 2.13, maximum 13.37 (b). Raw gaze gives 6.99 and 15.96. 54% to 97% of frames per mouse have a finite gaze.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Jitter-corrected CCGs during drifting gratings showed a significant sharp peak (within +/-10 ms and more than seven times the flank SD) for 16,119 of 2,089,890 possible cortical unit pairs, 0.96% +/- 0.13% per mouse in 25 mice.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 2; Extended Data Fig. 7b
outcomes.quote: yielding 16,119 pairs of units out of 2,089,890 possible pairs within the cortex ( Extended Data Fig. 7b ; 0.96% ± 0.13% per mouse, n = 25 mice)
outcomes.notes: No reading gives the three values within tolerance. Window 2 s and all non-noise units above 2 Hz (10,283 units in 26 mice); 21,962 sharp peaks of 2,116,259 pairs (pairs within tolerance, peaks above 16,119 +/- 1,612), 1.18% per mouse (SD 0.69%, s.e.m. 0.14%; above 0.96 +/- 0.13). The 3 s window gives 23,474 peaks; the Extended Data Fig. 1j filters give 544,044 pairs, far from the paper's 2,089,890. With any one mouse left out, 19,937 to 21,730 peaks and 1.10% to 1.22% per mouse. The round-1 result (17,592 peaks, within tolerance) came from an error in the expected CCG under jitter at negative lags, now fixed and checked against a direct enumeration of spike pairs. The paper's code subtracts one random jitter resample, which adds noise to the flanks; that variant was not run, as the jitter function it imports is not public.
deviations: 26 Functional Connectivity mice, where the paper uses 25; the one left out is not identified.

The jitter-corrected CCG subtracts the exact expected CCG under jitter of both trains within 25 ms windows (the Methods' true expected value); the paper's code subtracts one random resample (a variant the claims file names, not run because the jitter module get_ccgjitter imports is in neither repository the paper links).
Bin 1 ms, from the example in Figure2/compute_ccg.ipynb, as the claims file gives.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: In an example mouse, the CCG peak offsets between V1 and LM were shifted positive against the V1-V1 distribution (median 3.9 ms), so V1 units on average lead LM units.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 2; Fig. 2d
outcomes.quote: the peak offset distribution between V1 and LM showed a significant positive delay compared to the V1–V1 distribution ( Fig. 2d ; P = 2.6 × 10 −8 , two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test), indicating that V1 neurons ... lead LM neurons

statistics.n: V1-LM against V1-V1 peak offsets in one example mouse

outcomes.notes: Judged under 2 s and all units; every reading gives the same outcome. In 4 of 15 mice with both distributions the median V1 to LM offset is 4.0 ms with V1-LM above V1-V1 (rank-sum p < 1e-6); 14 of 15 medians are positive and 13 of 15 tests significant with V1-LM higher. The V1-V1 reference counts each pair once, in a random orientation; counted twice it also gives 4 mice, and every other reading at least 4. Offsets are whole ms.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Across 25 mice, the CCG peak offset distributions between neighbouring cortical areas differ from the within-area distributions for V1-LM, LM-RL, RL-AL and PM-AM, but not for AL-PM.
outcomes.source: Methods, Cross-correlation analysis, last paragraph; Fig. 2e legend

outcomes.statement: On average V1 units lead the units of the other cortical areas, while AM follows the other areas, placing AM at the top of the hierarchy.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 7c
outcomes.quote: On average, V1 units lead the activity of units in other areas ( Extended Data Fig. 7c , left column); by contrast, area AM follows other regions

The Extended Data Fig. 1j readings also give 9 of 10 and 3 s with all units 8 of 10 (V1 to RL -0.20 ms), all partial, so the outcome does not rest on the adopted reading.

outcomes.statement: The matrix of pairwise directionality scores between cortical areas is correlated with the matrix of anatomical hierarchy score differences (Pearson r = 0.74 over 21 pairs).
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 3; Fig. 2e, f
outcomes.quote: The matrix of pairwise directionality scores ( Fig. 2e ) between areas was very similar to the matrix of anatomical hierarchy score differences ( Fig. 2b ) (Pearson’s r = 0.74, P = 1 × 10 −4
outcomes.notes: 2 s, all units, DS from offsets pooled over mice; r = 0.827, p < 1e-5 over 21 entries, above the tolerance (0.666 to 0.814). The criterion names no partial outcome; the correlation is present and significant but stronger than the paper's, so the claim holds in part. With any one mouse left out r = 0.802 to 0.839, and 3 of the 26 exclusions (mice 820866111, 800250054, 763884096) give r within the tolerance (0.802 to 0.811); the paper used 25 mice and the one left out is not identified, so the outcome also rests on which 25 mice are used. Pooled DS under the other readings r = 0.800 to 0.842; the two Extended Data Fig. 1j readings (0.810, 0.800) are within the tolerance and 3 s with all units (0.842) is not. DS averaged across mice 0.777 to 0.817; zero lags counted positive 0.621 to 0.786. The paper's precomputed matrix gives r = 0.735 with the same anatomy differences.
deviations: Assumed; no reading reproduces fig2-sharp-peak-pairs, so the claims that use the sharp peaks are judged under all non-noise units and the 2 s window, the reading whose pair count matches the paper's and whose peak count is nearest it. The paper does not state either.
Within-area pairs enter both ways (offset and its negative), so the diagonal DS is 0; the paper's precomputed diagonal is near 0 (0.008 for V1).
All 26 Functional Connectivity mice are used, where the paper uses 25; 3 of the 26 single-mouse exclusions put r within the tolerance.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: The physical layout of the areas does not account for the correlation between directionality and hierarchy in terms of average distance.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 7e
outcomes.quote: The spatial layout of areas could not account for this correlation in terms of average physical distance
outcomes.notes: The claim needs the mean 3D CCF distance between units of each pair of areas. In every session file (58) and every probe file (325, 27,329 channels) of 000021 and 000022 the electrodes' y and z columns are identical, so the left-right coordinate is not in the files, and the six areas lie side by side across the cortex. A variant from the two coordinates present (anterior-posterior and dorsal-ventral), not judged, correlates with the hierarchy difference (r = 0.581, p = 0.006).
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: The functional hierarchy is absent during spontaneous activity (30 min grey screen), which suggests it reflects activity driven by bottom-up input.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 3; Extended Data Fig. 7f, g
outcomes.quote: this organization was absent during spontaneous activity ( Extended Data Fig. 7f , g )
outcomes.notes: During the 30 min grey screen, 7,326 sharp peaks of 2,116,259 pairs (94 to 547 per mouse; 21,962 during gratings). With all non-noise units the DS matrix averaged across mice correlates with the hierarchy differences; 2 s segments r = 0.497, p = 0.022; 3 s r = 0.484, p = 0.026; pooled DS r = 0.435 and 0.445 (p = 0.049, 0.043). With the Extended Data Fig. 1j filters it does not (r = 0.142, p = 0.54; r = 0.170, p = 0.46). The outcome rests on the unit set; the one whose pair count matches the paper's is adopted. With any one mouse left out the 2 s correlation stays significant in 26 of 26 (p 0.009 to 0.043) and the 3 s one in 24 of 26 (p up to 0.059). The result is borderline, and it is measured under a reading with 36% more sharp peaks during gratings than the paper's (21,962 against 16,119). The round-1 correlations (r = 0.50 to 0.60 under every reading) were partly an effect of the jitter error.
deviations: The spontaneous block is cut into consecutive 2 s or 3 s segments and the units are those selected during gratings; the paper does not say how it was done.

Assumed; the unit set is all non-noise units above 2 Hz, the reading whose pair count matches the paper's (fig2-sharp-peak-pairs). The paper does not state it, and the Extended Data Fig. 1j filters give the opposite outcome.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: The measured functional network has a total hierarchy score of 0.89, close to a simulated ladder-like hierarchy with feedback (0.88), above a one-to-all (0.15) or three-level (0.38) network and below a strongly feedforward one (1.54).
outcomes.source: Methods, Network model simulation; Extended Data Fig. 8
outcomes.quote: The maximum difference of this trajectory (here between V1 and AM) is defined as the total hierarchy score (THS) of the network, which is 0.89 for the measured functional network in our data ... The resulting DS matrix showed a gradient very similar to the real data, with a THS equal to 0.88
outcomes.notes: 2 s, all units, pooled DS; THS = 0.839, within 0.89 +/- 0.089 and between 0.15 and 1.54; V1 highest as source (0.447), AM lowest (-0.392). Without the diagonal 1.006; DS averaged across mice 0.727 (outside the tolerance); the other pooled readings 0.843 to 0.932. Every pooled reading is within the tolerance, so the outcome does not rest on the adopted reading.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

outcomes.statement: Within an area, superficial layers (2 to 4) are hierarchically lower than deep layers (5 and 6), with superficial layers tending to drive deep layers in the CCG analysis.
outcomes.source: Results, A functional hierarchy of visual areas, paragraph 5; Extended Data Fig. 10c to e
outcomes.quote: Analysis of layer-wise CCG interactions indicated that superficial layers (2/3 and 4) were hierarchically lower compared to deep layers (5, 6) in the same area
outcomes.notes: Superficial (layer codes 2, 4) to deep (5, 6) DS within an area, 2 s and all units; (a) 0.321, (b) 0.318, from 4,974 pairs; positive in every area (0.11 to 0.56) and under all four readings ((a) 0.220 to 0.321, (b) 0.264 to 0.318). 49 CCG units have no layer in the table.
outcomes.where: DANDI:000021 and DANDI:000022 (the paper's Data availability)

findings.statement: Dandiset 000253 names this paper as IsSupplementTo, but it holds the OpenScope Global/Local Oddball experiment (14 mice, oddball gratings, a 1,944-presentation receptive field mapping, optotagging) and none of the paper's recordings; it has no full-field flashes, no 81-location Gabor block of 3,645 presentations and no drifting gratings of 75 repeats. The paper's data are in dandisets 000021 and 000022, which its Data availability names.

In all 58 session files and all 325 probe files of 000021 and 000022 the electrodes table's y and z columns are identical on every channel, so one CCF coordinate (left-right) is missing. Distances between areas (Extended Data Fig. 7e) cannot be computed.

The units tables of 000021 and 000022 carry no stimulus metrics (p_value_rf, area_rf, mod_idx_dg, firing_rate_dg), which the paper's figure code reads from the AllenSDK. They were recomputed from the spike times as the Methods describe. The correlations with the hierarchy of Figure 3 are reproduced, but the hippocampal receptive field fraction is outside the paper's tolerance, per-unit latencies match the paper's table for at most 16% of units, and the pairwise modulation index tests (Extended Data Fig. 9e) are not reproduced.

The 21 behaviour sessions of Figure 4 (12 mice) are not deposited as recordings in any of the three dandisets, and the paper names no deposit; only metric tables are in its GitHub repository, so the behavioural performance (hit and false alarm rates) cannot be checked.

The Methods compute the time to first spike within 250 ms, the response decay timescale over 0 to 250 ms and the intrinsic timescale over the 1 s before each flash; the paper's scripts use 200 ms (get_flash_PSTH.py), 40 to 290 ms and 1.0 to 2.0 s after onset (timescale_calculation.py). The paper's timescale table matches the scripts' windows (99.3% and 99.6% of units within 1%). The windows change the unit counts of Figure 3 (13,344 against 17,163 after the latency cut) and the pairwise tests of Extended Data Fig. 9h.

No script of the paper's repository writes data/time_to_first_spike.csv; Figure3/get_flash_PSTH.py reads it and writes time_to_first_spike_20200312.csv. The table does not match latencies recomputed from the dandisets under any procedure tried (first spike from 30 ms, window ends 100 to 500 ms, all flashes, dark, light or one half, median or mean); at most 16% of units agree within 1 ms, median difference 4 ms, without bias.
The layer codes of the paper's layer_info.csv are not described; codes 2 and 4 are named L2/3 and L4 in ExtDataFigure10.py, while codes 1, 2 and 3 are also given to CA1, CA2 and CA3 units.

The CCG analyses use 25 mice of the Functional Connectivity set; 000022 holds 26, and the one left out is not identified (the code lists internal mouse ids that are not in the files). No single mouse left out changes the peak count outcome, but leaving out any of 3 of the 26 mice puts the DS correlation of Figure 2f within the paper's tolerance. The quality filter of the CCG units is not stated; the paper's pair count is matched with all non-noise units, not with the Extended Data Fig. 1j filters.

Question for the paper's authors - were Figure 3 and Extended Data Figs. 9 and 10 made with the Methods' windows (latency within 250 ms; decay timescale over 0 to 250 ms) or the scripts' (200 ms; 40 to 290 ms), and how was data/time_to_first_spike.csv computed? The unit counts of Figure 3 and three of the four layer differences of Extended Data Fig. 10b match only the scripts' windows or the paper's tables, and the pairwise decay tests (Extended Data Fig. 9h) depend on the window; this attempt judges the Methods' windows, as the claims file does.

Question for the paper's authors - which units entered the CCG analysis (the all_qc_meta files the code reads are not public), which CCG window was used (the 2 s presentation or the 3 s with grey), how the 30 min spontaneous block was cut into trials for Extended Data Fig. 7f, g, and which jitter function get_ccgjitter imports (the jitter module is in neither repository the paper links)? With all non-noise units and 2 s, which give the paper's pair count, this attempt finds 21,962 sharp peaks against 16,119, and a significant DS-hierarchy correlation during spontaneous activity, which the Extended Data Fig. 1j filters do not give.

Question for the paper's authors - how is the preferred condition of the modulation index defined (the AllenSDK metric the paper reads), in particular in the Functional Connectivity set where contrast varies? This attempt took the condition with the highest mean spike count.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebooks)
verifications.reviewed: Round 1. The executed notebooks with the conclusion cells and the summaries removed, the helper module and the claims file, with the paper. The verifier tested ccg_group against a brute-force jitter expectation on synthetic trains and checked the archive for the blocked claims. Its report had no attempt record and gave its own outcome for each claim; 34 of 36 agree with the round-1 record, with the eight tested CCG outcomes marked provisional because of the jitter error.

disagreements.reason: Under the claims' latency procedure, 13,347 or 24,481 units against 15,713 +/- 1,571, and 5,842 against 7,837 +/- 784 (cell 43). The code's 200 ms window (17,167 and 8,381) and the paper's tables both land within tolerance, but those are not the claims' reading.

All four differences have the right sign and p < 0.05, but only the RF area (105 deg2) is within tolerance. Latency 1.33 ms (expected 2.59 +/- 0.26), log10 MI 0.117 (0.09 +/- 0.009), decay 7.71 ms (6.6 +/- 0.66). One part out of four is below the two needed for partial (cell 49). In ed10b, 0.09 MI difference is fixed as log10 MI from the code; the paper's text says MI, and the raw-MI variant that the claims file lists was not run.

verifications.by: Independent agent run by CatalystNeuro (same harness, separate context, did not write the notebooks)
verifications.reviewed: Round 2. The full executed notebooks of the round-1 revision, the helper module, the claims file, the attempt record and the README, with the paper. The verifier agrees with all 36 outcomes, accepting fig2f and ed7fg as conditional. It reported stale numbers in the record, overstated sentences (the 'other' and selection_undocumented findings, CCG cell 36), a vacuous count in main cell 9, the README wording on the Figure 3 counts, and that the round-1 record said nine provisional CCG outcomes where it had marked eight. All are corrected, and the outputs it asked for are added.

entries.name: 000253-siegle-2021
entries.title: Survey of spiking in the mouse visual system (Siegle, Jia et al. 2021), from its DANDI deposits
entries.description: Tests the findings of Siegle, Jia et al. (2021) for dandiset 000253, which names the paper but holds a different experiment (the OpenScope Global/Local Oddball project). The passive viewing claims are tested on the paper's own deposits, dandisets 000021 and 000022 (58 sessions), with receptive fields, latencies, modulation indices, timescales and jitter-corrected cross-correlograms recomputed from the spike times, and the behaviour claims on the metrics tables of the paper's GitHub repository.
